source_text: Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν, οὐκ ἔστι τῶν πάντων οὐδὲν, ὃ μὴ διὰ τῆς ἀργίας ἀπόλλυται. Καὶ γὰρ ὕδωρ, τὸ μὲν ἑστηκὸς σήπεται, τὸ δὲ τρέχον καὶ πανταχοῦ πλανώμενον τὴν ἀρετὴν διασώζει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ· καὶ σίδηρος, ὁ μὲν ἐν ἀργίᾳ κείμενος, ἁπαλώτερός τε καὶ φαυλότερος, ἰῷ πολλῷ δαπανώμενος, γίνεται· ὁ δὲ ἐν ἐργασίαις ὢν, πολὺ χρησιμώτερος καὶ εὐπρεπέστερος, ἀργύρου παντὸς οὐδὲν ἔλαττον ἀποστίλβων. Καὶ γῆν μὲν τὴν ἀργοῦσαν ἴδοι τις ἂν οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς ἐκφέρουσαν, ἀλλὰ πονηρὰς βοτάνας καὶ ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους καὶ ἄκαρπα δένδρα, τὴν δὲ ἐργασίας ἀπολαύουσαν, καρποῖς ἡμέροις κομῶσαν. Καὶ ἕκαστον δὲ τῶν ὄντων, ὡς εἰπεῖν ἁπλῶς, ὑπὸ μὲν τῆς ἀργίας φθείρεται, ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς οἰκείας ἐργασίας χρησιμώτερον γίνεται. Ταῦτα οὖν εἰδότες ἅπαντα, καὶ πόσον μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ἀργίας τὸ βλάβος, πόσον δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐργασίας τὸ κέρδος, τὴν μὲν φεύγωμεν, τὴν δὲ διώκωμεν, ἵνα καὶ τὸν παρόντα βίον εὐσχημόνως ζήσωμεν, καὶ δεομένοις ἐκ τῶν ἐνόντων ἐπικουρήσωμεν, καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀμείνω κατασκευάσαντες τύχωμεν τῶν αἰωνίων ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος, ἅμα τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. ΕΙΣ ΑΚΥΛΑΝ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΙΣΚΙΛΛΑΝ Καὶ εἰς τὸ μὴ κακῶς λέγειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ. Λόγος βʹ. αʹ. Ἆρα ἐπαιδεύθητε μηδὲν εἶναι νομίζειν πάρεργον τῶν ἐν τῇ θείᾳ Γραφῇ κειμένων; ἆρα ἐμάθετε καὶ ἐπιγραφὰς καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ ψιλὰς περιεργάζεσθαι προσρήσεις, τὰς ἐν τοῖς θείοις Λογίοις γεγραμμένας; Ἐγὼ μὲν γὰρ οὐδένα οἶμαι λοιπὸν τῶν φιλοπόνων τὸν ἀνεξόμενον παραδραμεῖν τι τῶν ἐν ταῖς Γραφαῖς κειμένων ῥημάτων, κἂν ὀνομάτων ᾖ κατάλογος, κἂν χρόνων ἀριθμὸς, κἂν ψιλὴ πρός τινας πρόσρησις. Πλὴν ἵνα ἀσφαλεστέρα αὕτη ἡ διόρθωσις γένηται. φέρε καὶ τήμερον τὰ λειπόμενα τῆς προσηγορίας τῆς πρὸς Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν ἐπέλθωμεν· καίτοι γε οὐ μικρὰ τὸ προοίμιον αὐτῆς ἡμᾶς ὠφέλησε. Καὶ γὰρ ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς, πόσον μὲν ἀγαθὸν, ἔργον, πόσον δὲ κακὸν, ἀργία, καὶ τίς ἡ Παύλου ψυχὴ, πῶς ἄγρυπνος καὶ μεμεριμνημένη, οὐ κατὰ πόλεις καὶ δήμους καὶ ἔθνη, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθ' ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν πιστῶν πολλὴν ποιουμένη τὴν πρόνοιαν. Ἔδειξε πῶς οὐδὲν εἰς φιλοξενίαν ἡ πενία γίνεται κώλυμα, καὶ ὅτι οὐ πλούτου καὶ χρημάτων, ἀλλὰ ἀρετῆς πανταχοῦ χρεία καὶ προαιρέσεως εὐλάβειαν ἐχούσης, καὶ ὅτι πάντων εἰσὶ λαμπρότεροι οἱ τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φόβον ἔχοντες, κἂν εἰς πενίαν ἐσχάτην κατενεχθῶσι. Τὴν γοῦν Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν, σκηνοποιοὺς ὄντας καὶ χειροτέχνας, καὶ ἐν πτωχείᾳ ζῶντας, τῶν βασιλέων πάντων μᾶλλον ἐμακαρίζομεν νῦν· καὶ οἱ μὲν ἐν ἀξιώμασι καὶ δυναστείαις σεσίγηνται, ὁ δὲ σκηνοποιὸς μετὰ.30 τῆς γυναικὸς ᾄδονται πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης. Εἰ δὲ ἐνταῦθα τοσαύτης ἀπολαύουσι δόξης, ἐννόησον ὅσον κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην ἀξιωθήσονται τῶν ἀντιδόσεων καὶ τῶν στεφάνων· καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἡμέρας δὲ ἐκείνης, οὐ μικρὰν καὶ ἡδονὴν καὶ ὠφέλειαν καὶ δόξαν ἐκαρπώσαντο νῦν, Παύλῳ τοσοῦτον συζήσαντες χρόνον.
thought_title: Idleness corrupts all things; work preserves them
orientation: Chrysostom is concluding his argument that idleness destroys everything and work preserves it, then he transitions into the second homily on the greeting to Priscilla and Aquila.
pass_a_gloss: For there is not, there is not among all things anything, which is not destroyed through idleness. For indeed water, the standing water rots, but the running and everywhere wandering water preserves its own virtue; and iron, the iron lying in idleness, becomes both softer and more worthless, being consumed by much rust; but the iron being in works, much more useful and more comely, shining no less than all silver. And indeed the idle earth one might see producing nothing healthy, but wicked herbs and thorns and thistles and fruitless trees, but the earth enjoying work, abounding with cultivated fruits. And each of the things that exist, so to speak simply, is corrupted by idleness, but by its own work becomes more useful. Therefore knowing all these things, and how great is the harm from idleness, and how great is the gain from work, let us flee the one, and pursue the other, so that we may both live the present life decently, and help those in need from our resources, and having made our own soul better may obtain the eternal good things; of which may it be that all of us attain, by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen. ON AQUILA AND PRISCILLA And on not speaking evil of the priests of God. Homily 2. 1. Have you been taught to consider nothing of the things lying in the divine Scripture to be incidental? Have you learned to examine carefully even titles and names and bare greetings, the ones written in the divine Oracles? For I think no longer any of the diligent will endure to pass by any of the words lying in the Scriptures, even if it is a catalog of names, even if a number of times, even if a bare greeting to some people. But so that this correction may be more secure, come, let us also today go through the remaining parts of the address to Priscilla and Aquila; and indeed not small was the benefit its proem gave us. For it taught us, how great a good is work, and how great an evil is idleness, and what is the soul of Paul, how sleepless and full of care, making much provision not according to cities and peoples and nations, but also for each one of the faithful. It showed how poverty becomes no hindrance to hospitality, and that not of wealth and money, but of virtue everywhere there is need and of a disposition having piety, and that those having the fear of God are more splendid than all, even if they are brought down to extreme poverty. Priscilla then and Aquila, being tentmakers and artisans, and living in poverty, we now blessed more than all kings; and those in dignities and powers have been silenced, but the tentmaker with his wife are sung everywhere in the inhabited world. But if here they enjoy so much glory, consider how much on that day they will be deemed worthy of the recompenses and the crowns; and before that day, they reaped no small pleasure and benefit and glory now, having lived with Paul for so much time.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of ἀρετή as the quality or excellence proper to the water, matching the glossary's sense of virtue as excellence, and preserves the reflexive possessive.
Renders the plural ἐργασίαις literally as 'works' to preserve the contrast with idleness and the sense of active labor, rather than smoothing to a singular abstraction.
Keeps the participle ἀπολαύουσαν as 'enjoying' to convey the earth's active benefit from cultivation, and retains 'work' for ἐργασία per the glossary.

choices.english: to examine carefully even bare greetings
choices.why: Preserves ψιλὰς as 'bare' to convey that even greetings without apparent content deserve scrutiny, and renders περιεργάζεσθαι as 'examine carefully' to keep the intensive force.
rejected: to busy oneself with simple greetings

choices.why: Renders διόρθωσις literally as 'correction' to preserve Chrysostom's framing of the homily as a corrective teaching, rather than a neutral 'instruction'.
Keeps προαίρεσις as 'disposition' per the glossary and renders εὐλάβειαν as 'piety' to convey the reverent, cautious character of the disposition, preserving the participial construction.
rejected: of an intention having godly fear

pass_b_english: For there is nothing, nothing at all, that is not destroyed by idleness. Water that stands still rots, but water that runs and wanders everywhere preserves its own virtue. Iron that lies idle becomes softer and more worthless, consumed by heavy rust, but iron that is in works is far more useful and more beautiful, shining forth no less than any silver. You could see untilled earth producing nothing healthy, but only wicked weeds and thorns and thistles and fruitless trees, while earth enjoying work abounds with cultivated fruits. And each of the things that exist, to speak simply, is corrupted by idleness and becomes more useful through its own work. Since we know all these things, and how great is the harm from idleness and how great the gain from work, let us flee the one and pursue the other, so that we may live the present life with dignity, and help those in need from our own resources, and by making our own soul better may obtain the eternal good things. May it be granted to all of us to attain these, by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
On Aquila and Priscilla, and on not speaking evil of the priests of God. Homily 2.

Have you been taught to consider nothing in the divine Scripture incidental? Have you learned to examine carefully even titles and names and bare greetings written in the divine oracles? For I think that no one among the diligent will any longer endure passing over any of the words laid down in the Scriptures, whether it is a list of names, or a reckoning of years, or a bare greeting to certain people. But so that this correction may be made more secure, come, let us go through today what remains of the greeting to Priscilla and Aquila. And indeed its introduction has helped us not a little. For it taught us how great a good work is, and how great an evil idleness is, and what Paul's soul was like—how wakeful and full of care, making great provision not only for cities and peoples and nations, but also for each one of the faithful. It showed how poverty is no obstacle to hospitality, and that what is needed everywhere is not wealth and money but virtue and a disposition having piety, and that those who have the fear of God are more illustrious than all, even if they are brought down to extreme poverty. At any rate, we now count Priscilla and Aquila—tentmakers and manual laborers, living in poverty—more blessed than all the kings. Those in high rank and power are forgotten, but the tentmaker with his wife is sung everywhere throughout the inhabited world. And if they enjoy such glory here, consider how great the rewards and crowns they will be counted worthy of on that day. And even before that day, they have reaped no small pleasure and benefit and glory now, having lived with Paul for so long a time.

problems.quote: Those in dignities and powers have fallen silent
problems.source_quote: οἱ μὲν ἐν ἀξιώμασι καὶ δυναστείαις σεσίγηνται
problems.why: "fallen silent" is literal but misleading; means they are forgotten/uncelebrated, not literally silent.
problems.fix: Those in high rank and power are forgotten
problems.ruling: σεσίγηνται 'have fallen silent' misleads; context contrasts being sung vs. forgotten, not literal silence.

edits.old: Those in dignities and powers have fallen silent
edits.new: Those in high rank and power are forgotten

fixed: Changed 'fallen silent' to 'are forgotten' because σεσίγηνται here means they are passed over in silence, i.e., uncelebrated, not literally silent.

problems.why: In English 'a number of times' means 'several occasions'; the Greek means a reckoning of years or chronological numbers in Scripture.
problems.ruling: χρόνων ἀριθμὸς is scriptural year-counts or chronology, not colloquial English 'several occasions'.

edits.old: whether it is a list of names, or a number of times, or a bare greeting
edits.new: whether it is a list of names, or a reckoning of years, or a bare greeting

fixed: Fixed 'or a number of times' to 'or a reckoning of years': source κἂν χρόνων ἀριθμὸς means a number of years/chronology, not several occasions.

last_rejected.quote: water that runs and wanders everywhere preserves its own virtue
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ δὲ τρέχον καὶ πανταχοῦ πλανώμενον τὴν ἀρετὴν διασώζει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ
last_rejected.why: "wanders" suggests aimlessness; πλανώμενον means flowing/moving about, not wandering lost
last_rejected.fix: water that runs and flows everywhere preserves its own virtue
last_rejected.ruling: πλανώμενον means wandering/roaming; 'wanders' is within normal range, not misleading here.

last_rejected.why: "in works" is unidiomatic and obscure; means iron engaged in work/labor/use
last_rejected.fix: iron that is put to work
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν ἐργασίαις 'in works' is literal but intelligible; not a changed meaning.

last_rejected.why: εὐπρεπής here means seemly, proper, presentable—not beautiful; context is usefulness and appearance fitting its purpose
last_rejected.ruling: εὐπρεπής can mean beautiful/fair; 'more beautiful' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: ἀργοῦσαν means idle, not untilled; parallel to ἀργία throughout; misses the thematic link
last_rejected.fix: idle earth or land that lies idle
last_rejected.ruling: ἀργοῦσαν 'idle' applied to land naturally means untilled; not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: ἀπολαύουσαν means enjoying/partaking of, but "enjoying work" is ambiguous; means land that receives the benefit of work
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπολαύουσαν + gen. 'enjoying' is standard; 'enjoying work' conveys the meaning adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἡμέροις means tame, cultivated as opposed to wild—not "cultivated fruits" as a phrase
last_rejected.ruling: ἡμέροις means cultivated/tame; 'cultivated fruits' is a normal rendering.

last_rejected.why: οἰκείας means proper, appropriate, belonging to it—not "its own" in sense of possession
last_rejected.ruling: οἰκείας means 'its own/proper'; 'its own work' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: ἐκ τῶν ἐνόντων means from what is at hand, available—not specifically "our own resources"
last_rejected.fix: from what we have at hand
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκ τῶν ἐνόντων 'from what is at hand'; 'our own resources' is adequate paraphrase.

last_rejected.why: ἐπιγραφαί here means inscriptions, headings, possibly titles of psalms—not "titles" in modern sense
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιγραφάς can mean titles/headings; 'titles' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: χρόνων means times in sense of periods, dates, chronology—not "number of times" as frequency
last_rejected.fix: a number of dates or chronology
last_rejected.ruling: χρόνων ἀριθμός 'number of times/periods'; rendering is adequate, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: διόρθωσις means amendment, improvement, setting right—here likely "this course of improvement" or "this reform"
last_rejected.ruling: διόρθωσις means correction/amendment; 'correction' is standard and adequate.

last_rejected.why: προοίμιον means preface, preamble, prelude—refers to the previous homily/section, not "introduction" in abstract sense
last_rejected.ruling: προοίμιον means introduction/preface; 'introduction' is within normal range.
